blocks.html: In Grade 1 you learned Facts within 20 with tricks like making a ten and using doubles. Now the goal is to just know each fact, the way you know your own name. When facts come fast, your brain has room for bigger problems like $38 + 47$.

blocks.name: tenframe
blocks.cap: 8 red and 5 yellow counters. Press “Make a ten”: 2 yellow counters slide up, so $8 + 5 = 10 + 3$.

blocks.html: There are only 100 addition facts with one-digit numbers, from $0 + 0$ to $9 + 9$. Turn-around facts like $8 + 5$ and $5 + 8$ have the same answer, so there are only about half as many to learn. And every subtraction fact hides inside an addition fact: if you know $8 + 5 = 13$, you also know $13 - 5 = 8$ and $13 - 8 = 5$.

blocks.title: Use a double
steps: 8 is one more than 7, so the answer is one more: $15$.

blocks.name: numberbond
blocks.cap: A number bond for 14. One part is 6. What is the other part? Press “Show” to check.

blocks.html: Know each addition fact well, and you get the subtraction facts for free: if $a + b = c$, then $c - a = b$.
Counting on and saying the first number again. For $8 + 5$, some people count “8, 9, 10, 11, 12” and get 12. Start at the next number: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13. Quick check: $8 + 5$ is the same as $10 + 3$.
Grown-up tip: Five minutes a day beats an hour once a week. Mix in the facts your child misses, and praise careful thinking more than speed.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.OA.B.2 (add and subtract within 20 fluently; know sums of two one-digit numbers from memory)

blocks.html: Some groups can be shared fairly between two friends. Others always have one left over. Let’s find out which is which. Doubles will help.

blocks.name: g2-array
blocks.cap: 9 dots in pairs: 4 pairs and 1 dot left over (yellow). 9 is odd.

blocks.html: A number is even when you can put all of its objects in pairs, with none left over. It is odd when one is left over. Every even number is a double: $8 = 4 + 4$.

blocks.name: hundredchart
blocks.cap: The even numbers are shaded. Look down the columns: every even number ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

blocks.html: Why does only the ones digit matter? A ten is 5 pairs, so every ten pairs up with nothing left over. In 34, the 3 tens make 15 pairs. Only the 4 ones are left to pair, and 4 ones make 2 pairs. So 34 is even.

blocks.title: Is 13 even or odd?
steps: One is left over, so 13 is odd.

blocks.title: Is 58 even or odd?
steps: The 5 tens make 25 pairs. Don’t let the 5 fool you.
The ones digit is 8: 4 pairs, none left over.

blocks.title: Is 0 even or odd?
steps: Zero things: nothing is left over.
Counting by 2s goes 0, 2, 4, 6, … so 0 is even.

blocks.html: Even numbers make pairs with none left over and end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Odd numbers have one left over and end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.

Looking at the wrong digit: “52 is odd because 5 is odd.” The tens always pair up, so only the ones digit counts: 52 is even. Another mix-up is thinking 0 is neither. Zero is even, because $0 = 0 + 0$ and nothing is left over.
Grown-up tip: Pair up socks, shoes or crackers and ask, “Is there one without a partner?”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.OA.C.3 (decide whether a group of up to 20 objects has an odd or even number of members)

blocks.html: You know how to count by tens (Counting by Tens): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 … What comes next? 100! That is 10 tens.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Tap the tens column (or the trade button) to bundle 10 tens into 1 hundred flat.

blocks.html: We bundle by tens again and again. 10 ones make 1 ten. 10 tens make 1 hundred. A hundred flat is exactly 10 ten-rods side by side, so it is the same amount, just packed into one piece. Bundling lets us count big piles quickly.

blocks.title: Hundreds with zeros
blocks.q: Write the number for 7 hundreds, 0 tens and 0 ones.
steps: There are no tens or ones, so write 0 in both of those places.

blocks.title: More than 10 tens
steps: 2 tens are left over: that is 20.

blocks.html: 10 ones make 1 ten, and 10 tens make 1 hundred. The numbers 100, 200, 300, … 900 mean 1, 2, 3, … 9 hundreds, with 0 tens and 0 ones.
Thinking 300 has 3 tens. The 3 in 300 means 3 hundreds, and each hundred is 10 tens, so 300 has 30 tens. Check with money: 3 one-dollar bills are worth the same as 30 dimes.
Grown-up tip: Bundle straws or craft sticks with rubber bands: 10 singles in a bundle, then 10 bundles in a big bundle.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.A.1a (100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens, called a hundred)
Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.A.1b (100, 200, … 900 refer to one to nine hundreds, 0 tens and 0 ones)

blocks.html: Now you can build any number up to 999 with three kinds of blocks: hundreds (flats), tens (rods) and ones (small cubes). It works just like Tens and Ones, with one more place.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: 352 is 3 hundreds, 5 tens and 2 ones. Use − and + to build other numbers.

blocks.html: Each place holds only 0 to 9 of something, because 10 of anything gets bundled into the next place. So a three-digit number has exactly one digit for hundreds, one for tens and one for ones. The place of a digit tells what it is worth: in 352, the 3 is worth 300, the 5 is worth 50 and the 2 is worth 2.

blocks.title: Read the blocks
blocks.q: What number is 2 hundreds, 4 tens and 7 ones?
steps: Write one digit in each place: 247.

blocks.title: A zero holds a place
blocks.q: What number is 3 hundreds and 4 ones?
steps: There are no tens, so write 0 in the tens place to hold it.

blocks.title: What is a digit worth?
steps: The 6 is in the tens place.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Your turn: build 304. How many tens do you need?

blocks.html: In a three-digit number, the digits stand for hundreds, tens and ones, from left to right. A 0 holds a place when there are none of that kind.

Writing 3 hundreds and 4 ones as 34 or 3004. But 34 means 3 tens and 4 ones, and 3004 is more than three thousand. Check: a number in the hundreds has exactly three digits, and the middle one tells the tens.
Grown-up tip: Read numbers on house doors, book pages or price tags together, and ask what each digit is worth.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.A.1 (the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens and ones)
OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, Section 1.1 Introduction to Whole Numbers (background for grown-ups)

blocks.html: Skip counting means counting by the same jump each time. You already count by tens (Counting by Tens). Now count by 5s, 10s and 100s, starting from any number up to 1,000.

blocks.name: hundredchart
blocks.cap: Counting by 5s: every shaded number ends in 5 or 0.

blocks.html: Adding 10 adds one more ten, so only the tens digit goes up by 1. Adding 100 adds one more hundred, so only the hundreds digit goes up. Adding 5 to a number that ends in 0 or 5 makes the ones digit flip: 0, 5, 0, 5.

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: Ten jumps of 100 reach 1,000.

blocks.title: Count by 10s across a hundred
steps: 10 more than 490 makes 10 tens, which is a new hundred.

blocks.html: Skip counting adds the same amount each time. Counting by 10s changes the tens digit; counting by 100s changes the hundreds digit.
After 490, writing “4100.” The tens place can’t hold 10. When the tens reach 10, they make a new hundred: $490 + 10 = 500$.
Grown-up tip: Count nickels by 5s and dimes by 10s, or count by 100s as you climb the stairs.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.A.2 (count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s and 100s)

blocks.html: There are three ways to write a number. They all show the same amount. You will need Hundreds, Tens and Ones for this.

head: Digits
Words
Expanded form
blocks.cap: Three ways to write the same numbers.

blocks.name: placevalue
blocks.cap: The chart shows 406 in expanded form and in words. Use the ▲ and ▼ arrows to change a digit.

blocks.html: Expanded form shows what each digit is worth, added together. Words say the hundreds first, then the rest: “four hundred” is 400, and “six” is 6. There are no tens, so the tens place gets a 0 when you write the digits.

blocks.title: Words to digits
steps: “Seven hundred” means 7 in the hundreds place.
“Eight” means 8 ones. No tens are said, so the tens digit is 0.

blocks.title: Expanded form in any order
steps: 900 is 9 hundreds, 30 is 3 tens and 4 is 4 ones.
Put each digit in its place: 934.

blocks.html: Digits, words and expanded form are three ways to write the same number. Expanded form adds up what each digit is worth.
Writing “four hundred six” as 4006, by writing 400 and then 6 side by side. 4006 has four digits, so it is in the thousands. Check: a number in the hundreds has exactly three digits.
Grown-up tip: Say a number out loud and let your child write it, then switch roles.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.A.3 (read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form)

blocks.html: You compared two-digit numbers in Grade 1 (Comparing Two-Digit Numbers). Bigger numbers work the same way: start with the biggest place.

blocks.name: g2-blocks
blocks.cap: 312: 3 hundreds, 1 ten and 2 ones.

blocks.name: g2-blocks
blocks.cap: 299: 2 hundreds, 9 tens and 9 ones. Which number is more?

blocks.html: One hundred is more than any number of tens and ones you can write with two digits: even 99 is 1 less than 100. So if one number has more hundreds, it is bigger, no matter what its other digits are. Only when the hundreds match do you look at the tens, and only when the tens match do you look at the ones.

blocks.title: Different hundreds
steps: Stop here: 312 is bigger, even though 299 has bigger tens and ones.

blocks.title: Expanded form
steps: The hundreds are the same. Tens: 0 tens and 9 tens.

blocks.html: Compare the hundreds first, then the tens, then the ones. Write $>$ (greater than), $<$ (less than) or $=$ (equal). The open side of $>$ or $<$ faces the bigger number.
Picking the number with the biggest digits. 299 has two 9s, but 312 is bigger, because 3 hundreds beat 2 hundreds. Check: which number needs more hundred flats to build?
Grown-up tip: Compare page numbers or prices, and ask, “Which place did you look at first?”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.A.4 (compare two three-digit numbers based on the hundreds, tens and ones digits, using >, = and <)

blocks.html: A number line is like a ruler for numbers. The marks are spaced evenly, so every jump from one mark to the next is the same size. Skip counting (Skip Counting by 5s, 10s and 100s) helps you read it.

blocks.name: g2-line
blocks.cap: Only 300 and 400 are labeled. What number is the dot?

blocks.html: From 300 to 400 is 100. There are 10 equal jumps, and 10 jumps of 10 make 100, so each jump is 10. Now count jumps from 300: 310, 320, 330, 340, 350, 360, 370. The dot is 7 jumps along, at 370.

blocks.title: Find the jump size
blocks.q: A number line goes from 0 to 1,000 in 10 equal jumps. How big is each jump?
steps: That takes 10 jumps, so each jump is 100.

blocks.title: Count jumps, not marks
blocks.q: Each jump is 10. A dot is 4 jumps after 50. Where is it?
steps: Start at 50. Don’t count the 50 mark itself.

blocks.name: g2-line
blocks.cap: Only 600 and 610 are labeled. Find the jump size first, then find the dot.

blocks.html: On a number line every jump is the same size. Find the jump size first, then count jumps, not marks.
Counting the tick marks instead of the jumps. If you count the starting mark as “1,” you end up one jump too far. Check: put your finger on the start, then count each hop to the next mark.
Grown-up tip: Draw a number line on a long strip of paper and let your child hop a toy along it.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.B.6 (represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line with equally spaced points)

blocks.html: In Grade 1 you found 10 More and 10 Less for two-digit numbers. With hundreds you can also find 100 more and 100 less, in your head.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: 245. Press + under Tens for 10 more, or + under Hundreds for 100 more. Watch which digit changes.

blocks.html: 10 more means one more ten-rod, so only the tens digit changes. 100 more means one more hundred-flat, so only the hundreds digit changes. The other blocks did not move, so their digits stay the same.

blocks.title: 10 more
steps: One more ten: 6 tens become 7 tens.

blocks.title: 100 less
steps: One less hundred: 4 hundreds become 3 hundreds.

blocks.title: Crossing a hundred
steps: 395 has 9 tens. One more makes 10 tens.
10 tens make 1 hundred, so the hundreds go from 3 to 4 and the tens become 0.

blocks.name: hundredchart
blocks.cap: A chart from 301 to 400. Move the marker down one row for 10 more, or up one row for 10 less.

blocks.html: To add or take away 10, change the tens digit by 1. To add or take away 100, change the hundreds digit by 1.
Writing 10 more than 395 as 3105. The tens place can’t hold 10: ten tens make a new hundred, so the answer is 405. Check with blocks: 39 tens and 1 more ten is 40 tens, which is 400, plus 5.
Grown-up tip: Play “10 more, 100 less” with house numbers on a walk.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.B.8 (mentally add 10 or 100 to a number 100–900, and mentally subtract 10 or 100)

blocks.html: When you made a new ten in Grade 1 (Adding That Makes a New Ten), you traded 10 ones for 1 ten. Let’s look closely at why that trade is fair, because every carry and every borrow is this same trade.

blocks.name: base10

task.text: Trade 10 ones for 1 ten, so no place has more than 9.

blocks.cap: 3 tens and 14 ones. Tap the ones (or the trade button) to trade 10 ones for 1 ten.

blocks.html: A ten-rod is just 10 ones stuck together. Trading 10 loose ones for 1 rod is like trading 10 pennies for a dime: you have the same amount, packed a different way. Nothing was added and nothing was lost. Breaking a ten into 10 ones is the same trade, done backward.

blocks.title: Trade ones for a ten
blocks.q: What number is 3 tens and 14 ones?
steps: Trade 10 ones for 1 ten: now 4 tens and 4 ones.

blocks.title: Break a ten
steps: Break 1 ten into 10 ones: 4 tens and 12 ones.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Your turn: show 52 using exactly 4 tens. Tap a ten to break it into ones.

blocks.html: 10 ones = 1 ten, and 10 tens = 1 hundred. Trading or breaking changes how a number is shown, never how much it is.
Thinking a trade changes the number, so you stop trusting your answer. Check by finding the value both ways: 3 tens and 14 ones is $30 + 14 = 44$, and 4 tens and 4 ones is $40 + 4 = 44$.
Grown-up tip: Trade coins at home: 10 pennies for 1 dime. Count both piles to see that they match.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.B.9 (explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value)
Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.A.1a (a hundred is a bundle of ten tens)

blocks.html: To add two-digit numbers, add ones to ones and tens to tens. When the ones make 10 or more, trade them for a new ten, just like in Trading 10 Ones for 1 Ten.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Press “Add 47”, then trade 10 ones for a ten. How many tens and ones are there now?

blocks.html: Adding means putting all the blocks together. 8 ones and 7 ones make 15 ones, too many for one digit. Trade 10 of them for a new ten: now there is 1 more ten and 5 ones. The new ten must be counted with the other tens.

blocks.title: With a trade
steps: Ones: $8 + 7 = 15$. That is 1 ten and 5 ones. Write 5 and keep the new ten.

blocks.html: Add the ones, then the tens. If the ones make 10 or more, trade 10 ones for a new ten and add it to the tens.
Forgetting the new ten: $38 + 47 = 75$. The 15 ones held a hidden ten. Check by estimating: 38 is close to 40 and 47 is close to 50, so the sum is close to 90, not 75.
Grown-up tip: Ask your child where the little “1” comes from. If they can say “it’s the new ten,” they understand regrouping.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.B.5 (fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value)
OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, Section 1.2 Add Whole Numbers (background for grown-ups)

blocks.html: To subtract, take ones from ones and tens from tens. Sometimes there aren’t enough ones. Then you break a ten into 10 ones (Trading 10 Ones for 1 Ten).

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Press “Take away 27”. There are only 2 ones, so break a ten first: tap the tens.

blocks.html: 52 is 5 tens and 2 ones. You can’t take 7 ones away from 2 ones. Break one ten into 10 ones: now 52 is 4 tens and 12 ones. It is still 52, but now there are enough ones to take 7 away.

blocks.title: Break a ten
steps: Ones: 2 is less than 7. Break a ten: 4 tens and 12 ones.

blocks.title: Count up
steps: Start at 27. Jump 3 to get to 30.

blocks.html: Subtract the ones, then the tens. If there are not enough ones, break a ten into 10 ones first. Check by adding your answer to the number you took away.

Taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in each place: for $52 - 27$, doing $7 - 2 = 5$ and $5 - 2 = 3$ to get 35. But you must take 7 away from 2, so break a ten. Check: $35 + 27 = 62$, not 52, so 35 can’t be right.
Grown-up tip: Have your child check every subtraction by adding. It catches most mistakes.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.B.5 (fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value)
OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, Section 1.3 Subtract Whole Numbers (background for grown-ups)

blocks.html: Sometimes you add three or four numbers, like the points in a game. Place value still works: add all the tens, add all the ones, then put them together. You already know Adding Two-Digit Numbers.

blocks.name: g2-blocks
blocks.cap: 23, 14, 31 and 12 in four colors. How many tens are there? How many ones?

blocks.html: You can add numbers in any order and get the same total (Adding in Any Order). So you can gather all the tens first and all the ones first. Looking for ones that make 10 makes it even easier.

blocks.title: Lots of ones
steps: Ones: $7 + 8 + 9 + 5 = 29$. That is 2 tens and 9 ones.

blocks.html: To add several numbers, add all the tens, add all the ones, then combine. Look for ones that make 10.
Leaving a number out, or forgetting that the ones can make two new tens. Check: touch each number as you add it, and see whether the ones add to more than 19.
Grown-up tip: Keep score in a board game and add up each player’s points together.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.B.6 (add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value)

blocks.html: A number line turns adding and subtracting into jumps: jump right to add and left to subtract. You learned to read number lines in Numbers on a Number Line.

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: $46 + 27$ as jumps: +10, +10, then +4 to reach 70, then +3 to land on 73.

blocks.html: 27 is 2 tens and 7 ones, so you can jump 10, 10 and then 7. Splitting the 7 into 4 and 3 lands on 70 first, a friendly number. All the jumps together still add up to 27.

blocks.title: Add with jumps
steps: Start at 46. Jump +10 to 56, then +10 to 66.

blocks.title: Find the distance
blocks.q: How far is it from 58 to 92?

blocks.html: On a number line, adding jumps right and subtracting jumps left. Jump by tens, then ones, and aim for friendly numbers that end in 0.
Counting how many jumps there are instead of adding their sizes. From 58 to 92 there are 3 jumps, but they are 2, 30 and 2, so the distance is 34. Check: $58 + 34 = 92$.
Grown-up tip: A tape measure on the floor makes a great number line to hop along.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.B.6 (represent sums and differences within 100 on a number line diagram)

blocks.html: Word problems are little stories. Before you add or subtract, picture what happens. This builds on How Many More? How Many Fewer? and the stories you solved in Grade 1.

items: Put together: two parts make a whole.
Compare: how many more, or how many fewer?

blocks.html: A tape diagram shows the parts and the whole. If you know both parts, add to find the whole. If you know the whole and one part, subtract to find the other part. The picture decides what to do, not a single word in the story.

blocks.title: The start is missing
blocks.q: Some birds sat on a fence. Then 18 more birds landed. Now there are 45 birds. How many were on the fence at first?
steps: The story says “more,” but the start is the missing part.

blocks.name: tapediagram
blocks.cap: The birds: the whole is 45, one part is 18. Press “Next step”.

blocks.title: “Fewer,” but you add
blocks.q: Ana has 34 stickers. She has 12 fewer stickers than Ben. How many stickers does Ben have?
steps: “Ana has 12 fewer than Ben” means Ben has 12 more than Ana.
Ben’s amount is the bigger one: $34 + 12 = 46$.

blocks.name: tapediagram

steps: Ana has 34. Ben has the same as Ana and 12 more.
Ben’s amount is the whole top tape: 34 + 12 = 46.

blocks.cap: Ben’s tape is as long as Ana’s, plus 12 more. Press “Next step”.

blocks.html: Picture the story and find the whole and the parts. Whole missing: add. Part missing: subtract. Put your answer back into the story to check it.

Choosing the operation from a key word, like adding whenever you see “more.” In the bird story, “more” is there but you subtract. Check: put your answer into the story and read it again. Does it make sense?
Grown-up tip: Act the story out with toys, and ask your child to draw the tape before doing any math.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.OA.A.1 (use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems)

blocks.html: Some stories need two steps. First find a number the story doesn’t tell you. Then use it to answer the question. Each step is a one-step problem like the ones in Word Problems within 100.

blocks.title: Shells
blocks.q: Mia has 24 shells. Leo has 9 more shells than Mia. How many shells do they have together?
steps: Step 1: how many does Leo have? 24 + 9 = 33.

blocks.name: tapediagram

steps: Step 1: Leo has Mia’s 24 and 9 more: 24 + 9 = 33.

blocks.cap: Step 1 finds Leo’s 33 shells. Step 2 adds Mia’s 24. Press “Next step”.

blocks.html: The question asks about both children, but the story only tells you how many Mia has. You need Leo’s number before you can answer. That hidden middle number is what step 1 finds.

blocks.title: A bus
blocks.q: A bus has 35 people. At the first stop, 12 people get off and 8 get on. How many people are on the bus now?

blocks.html: In a two-step problem, find the hidden middle number first, then answer the question that was asked.
Stopping after step 1. In the shells story, 33 is Leo’s number, not the answer. Check: read the question again. It asks about both children, so the answer must be more than either child’s number.
Grown-up tip: Before any math, ask, “What do we need to know first?”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.OA.A.1 (use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems)

blocks.html: Adding three-digit numbers is like adding two-digit numbers, with one more place: the hundreds. Add the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Press “Add 258”. Trade 10 ones for a ten, then 10 tens for a hundred.

blocks.html: Each place holds 0 to 9. When the ones make 10 or more, 10 ones become a new ten. When the tens make 10 or more, 10 tens become a new hundred. Trading keeps the total the same and lets each place hold just one digit.

blocks.title: Two trades
steps: Ones: $7 + 8 = 15$. Write 5 and make a new ten.
Tens: $6 + 5 + 1 = 12$ tens. Write 2 and make a new hundred.

blocks.html: Add ones, tens, then hundreds. When a place gets 10 or more, trade 10 of them for 1 of the next place.

Squeezing a two-digit sum into one place. For $247 + 138$, the ones make $7 + 8 = 15$. Writing all of 15 in the answer gives 3715. A place holds only one digit: write 5 and trade the ten. The answer is 385. Check: 247 is close to 250 and 138 is close to 140, so the sum is close to 390, not thousands.
Grown-up tip: Graph paper helps keep the digits lined up in their places.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.B.7 (add and subtract within 1000 using models and strategies based on place value)
OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, Section 1.2 Add Whole Numbers (background for grown-ups)

blocks.html: Subtract the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds. If a place is short, break one from the next place: a ten into 10 ones, or a hundred into 10 tens. You did this with tens in Subtracting Two-Digit Numbers.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Press “Take away 175”. You will need to break a ten and then a hundred.

blocks.html: Breaking a hundred into 10 tens is a fair trade, just like breaking a ten into 10 ones. 5 hundreds and 3 tens is the same amount as 4 hundreds and 13 tens. But the hundred you broke is gone from the hundreds place, so that digit goes down by 1.

blocks.title: Break twice
steps: Ones: 2 is less than 5. Break a ten: 2 tens and 12 ones. $12 - 5 = 7$.
Tens: 2 is less than 7. Break a hundred: 4 hundreds and 12 tens. $12 - 7 = 5$.

blocks.title: Zeros
steps: There are no ones or tens to break, so break a hundred: 3 hundreds and 10 tens.
Now break a ten: 9 tens and 10 ones.

blocks.html: Subtract place by place. When a place is short, break a ten or a hundred, and lower the digit you broke it from. Add to check.
Breaking a hundred but forgetting to lower the hundreds digit, so $532 - 175$ comes out as 457. After the break there are only 4 hundreds. Check by adding: $457 + 175 = 632$, not 532.
Grown-up tip: Ask your child to cross out the digit they broke from and write the new digit above it.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.B.7 (add and subtract within 1000; sometimes it is necessary to decompose tens or hundreds)
OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, Section 1.3 Subtract Whole Numbers (background for grown-ups)

blocks.html: You know several ways to add and subtract (Adding Three-Digit Numbers, Subtracting Three-Digit Numbers). A good mathematician can also say why a way works.

blocks.title: Split by place value
steps: Why it works: these are the same blocks, sorted by kind.

blocks.title: Make a friendly number
steps: Why it works: nothing was added or lost, just moved.

blocks.title: Take too many, give some back
steps: You took away 2 too many, so give 2 back: $303 + 2 = 305$.

blocks.name: g2-line
blocks.cap: Counting up from 274 to 600: jumps of 6, 20 and 300 make 326, so $600 - 274 = 326$.

blocks.html: Every fair strategy keeps the amount the same. Splitting by place value only sorts the blocks. Moving 2 from one number to the other doesn’t change the total. Counting up works because subtraction tells how far apart two numbers are.
A strategy works when it keeps the total the same. You can show why with blocks or a number line, and check by doing the opposite operation.

Fixing up in the wrong direction. For $503 - 198$, some people take away 200 and then take away 2 more, getting 301. But you already took away too many, so you add 2 back: 305. Check: $305 + 198 = 503$.
Grown-up tip: Ask, “How do you know?” and let your child explain with blocks, coins or a drawing.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.NBT.B.9 (explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations)

blocks.html: In Grade 1 you measured with same-size units laid end to end (Measuring with Same-Size Units). A ruler is a row of units already laid out for you.

blocks.name: g2-ruler
blocks.cap: Slide the pencil. Wherever it goes, it covers the same 5 spaces.

blocks.html: Each number on a ruler tells how many units there are from the 0 mark. The first inch is the space from 0 to 1, not the mark at 1. So if one end of an object is at 0, the number at the other end is its length. If it isn’t at 0, count the spaces under the object.

blocks.title: Starting at 0
blocks.q: A crayon starts at 0 and ends at 4 on a centimeter ruler. How long is it?
steps: Read the number at the other end: 4.

blocks.title: Not starting at 0
blocks.q: A pencil lies from the 2 mark to the 7 mark on an inch ruler. How long is it?
steps: Count the spaces: 2 to 3, 3 to 4, 4 to 5, 5 to 6, 6 to 7.

blocks.html: Line up one end with 0 and read the number at the other end. If it isn’t at 0, count the spaces (the units), not the marks.
Lining the object up with the 1 mark instead of the 0 mark. Then every length comes out one too many. Check: count the spaces under the object with your finger.
Grown-up tip: Many rulers have a little extra edge before the 0. Show your child where 0 really is.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.A.1 (measure the length of an object with rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks and measuring tapes)

blocks.html: You can measure the same thing with different units: inches or centimeters, feet or yards. The length doesn’t change, but the number does. You need Measuring with a Ruler for this.

blocks.name: g2-ruler
blocks.cap: The same straw is 4 inches long and about 10 centimeters long.

blocks.html: A centimeter is shorter than an inch, so it takes more centimeters to cover the straw. A big unit covers more length each time, so you need fewer of them. Small unit, big number. Big unit, small number.

head: Bigger unit
is the same as
blocks.cap: Units that fit together exactly.

blocks.title: Feet to inches
blocks.q: A board is 2 feet long. How many inches is that?
steps: 2 feet and 24 inches are the same length.

blocks.title: Which is longer?
blocks.q: Which is longer: 30 inches or 2 feet?
steps: Change to the same unit: 2 feet is 24 inches.

blocks.html: The bigger the unit, the fewer you need. To compare two lengths, change them to the same unit first.
Thinking 24 inches is longer than 2 feet because 24 is a bigger number. They are exactly the same length! Check by changing to the same unit: 2 feet = 24 inches.
Grown-up tip: Measure a table with a ruler in inches and again with a yardstick, and compare the two numbers.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.A.2 (measure an object twice with different units and describe how the measurements relate to the size of the unit)

blocks.html: An estimate is a smart guess. You can estimate a length by comparing it with lengths you already know, then check by measuring (Measuring with a Ruler).

head: Unit
About as long as
rows: the width of your little finger
a ruler, or a sheet of paper (11 inches)
a big step for a grown-up
a little more than a yard
blocks.cap: Benchmarks to carry in your head.

blocks.html: If you know about how long 1 inch is, you can picture inch after inch along an object and count them. An estimate also helps you catch mistakes: if a ruler seems to say a pencil is 70 inches long, you know something went wrong.

blocks.name: g2-ruler
blocks.cap: Ava guessed 10 centimeters. The crayon is 9 centimeters long, so her estimate was close.

blocks.title: Pick a sensible estimate
blocks.q: About how tall is a classroom door: 2 centimeters, 2 meters or 20 meters?
steps: A door is taller than a grown-up.
2 centimeters is tiny, and 20 meters is taller than a house.

blocks.title: Choose the unit
blocks.q: Would you measure a soccer field in centimeters or meters?
steps: A soccer field is very long.
Meters are the bigger unit, so the number stays easy to use.

blocks.html: Estimate by comparing with a length you know. Use small units for small things and big units for big things.
Choosing the right number with the wrong unit, like “a pencil is 7 feet long.” Check: picture the unit. A foot is about as long as a ruler, and no pencil is 7 rulers long. It is about 7 inches.
Grown-up tip: Before you measure anything together, ask for a guess first, then see how close it was.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.A.3 (estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimeters and meters)

blocks.html: To compare two lengths, find how much longer one is than the other. Line them up at the same start and look at the extra piece. You will use Subtracting Two-Digit Numbers.

blocks.name: g2-ruler
blocks.cap: The ribbon is 9 centimeters long and the crayon is 5 centimeters long.

blocks.html: When two things start at the same place, the longer one sticks out past the shorter one. That extra piece is the difference, and subtraction finds it: the longer length minus the shorter length.

blocks.title: Ribbon and crayon
blocks.q: How much longer is the ribbon than the crayon?

blocks.title: Bigger numbers
blocks.q: A red rope is 62 inches long. A blue rope is 38 inches long. How much longer is the red rope?
steps: Count up from 38: +2 to 40, +20 to 60, +2 to 62.

blocks.name: tapediagram
blocks.cap: The extra piece of the red tape is the difference. Press “Next step”.

blocks.html: How much longer? Subtract the shorter length from the longer one. Both lengths must be in the same unit.
Adding the two lengths. $62 + 38 = 100$ tells how long the ropes are end to end, not how much longer one is. Check: the difference must be smaller than the longer length.
Grown-up tip: Line up two shoes, two pencils or two toy cars, and ask how much longer one is.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.A.4 (measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, in a standard length unit)

blocks.html: Length stories use the same thinking as other word problems, with units like inches or meters. Keep the unit with your answer.

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: Boards of 34 inches and 28 inches, end to end, reach 62 inches.

blocks.html: A length is like a distance on a number line. Putting things end to end adds their lengths. Cutting a piece off takes length away. Comparing two lengths finds the difference.

blocks.title: End to end
blocks.q: Two boards are 34 inches and 28 inches long. They are placed end to end. How long are they together?
steps: End to end means the lengths join: add.

blocks.title: Cut off
blocks.q: A rope is 80 centimeters long. Sam cuts off 35 centimeters. How long is the rope now?
steps: Cutting off makes it shorter: subtract.

blocks.title: The start is missing
blocks.q: Pat cut 18 inches off a ribbon. Now 47 inches are left. How long was the ribbon at first?
steps: The first ribbon is the whole. The 18 cut off and the 47 left are its parts.

blocks.html: Draw the lengths as jumps on a number line or as a tape. Add when lengths join; subtract when length is cut off or compared. Use one unit.
Mixing units. 1 foot and 6 inches is not “7” of anything. Change to one unit first: 1 foot is 12 inches, so 1 foot and 6 inches is 18 inches.
Grown-up tip: Use a measuring tape for real problems: How much ribbon do we need for two bows?

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.B.5 (use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths in the same units)

blocks.html: You can read times like 3:00 and 3:30 (Time to the Hour and Half Hour). Now you will read the long hand anywhere on the clock, by counting by 5s (Skip Counting by 5s, 10s and 100s).

blocks.name: clock
blocks.cap: The red numbers around the outside show the minutes. The long hand points to the 4, and four 5s are 20: it is 3:20.

blocks.html: The long minute hand goes all the way around in 60 minutes. The clock has 12 numbers, and 12 jumps of 5 make 60: 5, 10, 15, … 60. So each number stands for 5 more minutes. The short hand moves slowly from one hour to the next during that time.

blocks.title: Read 3:20
blocks.q: The short hand is a bit past 3. The long hand points to the 4.
steps: The short hand has passed 3 but not reached 4, so the hour is 3.
Long hand on the 4: count by 5s four times: 5, 10, 15, 20.

blocks.title: Almost the next hour
blocks.q: The short hand is almost at the 9. The long hand points to the 9.
steps: The short hand has not reached 9 yet, so the hour is still 8.
Long hand on the 9: nine 5s are 45 minutes.

blocks.name: clock
blocks.cap: Your turn: show 8:45. Drag the long hand to the 9 and look where the short hand goes.

blocks.html: The short hand shows the hour it has passed. For the long hand, count by 5s for each number, starting at the 12.
Reading the number the long hand points to as the minutes, like saying 3:04 when it is 3:20. The 4 means four 5s. Check: when the long hand points to the 6, it is halfway around, which is 30 minutes.
Grown-up tip: Ask what time it is on a clock with hands a few times a day, and count the 5s out loud together.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.C.7 (tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m.)

blocks.html: The short hand goes around the clock twice each day. So 7:00 happens two times: once in the morning and once in the evening. We write a.m. or p.m. to tell them apart. You need Time to Five Minutes for this.

blocks.name: clock
blocks.cap: Press “+ 1 hour” again and again. Watch a.m. change to p.m. at 12 noon.

blocks.html: A day starts at midnight. The a.m. hours run from midnight to noon: night and morning. The p.m. hours run from noon to midnight: afternoon, evening and night. Noon is 12:00 p.m. and midnight is 12:00 a.m.

head: What happens
a.m. or p.m.?
blocks.cap: One school day.

blocks.title: Crossing noon
blocks.q: A field trip starts at 10:00 a.m. and lasts 3 hours. When does it end?
steps: Count on one hour at a time: 11:00 a.m., 12:00 noon, 1:00 p.m.
After noon, a.m. changes to p.m.

blocks.html: a.m. is from midnight to noon. p.m. is from noon to midnight.
Calling lunch at 12:15 “a.m.” because the hour is 12. Noon starts the p.m. hours, so 12:15 in the daytime is p.m. Check: is it before noon or after?
Grown-up tip: Point out a.m. and p.m. on a phone or an oven clock.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.C.7 (tell and write time to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m.)

blocks.html: Here are the coins you will use most: the penny, nickel, dime and quarter. Each one is worth some cents (¢). Counting by 5s and 10s (Skip Counting by 5s, 10s and 100s) will help.

blocks.name: coins
blocks.cap: Coins at their real sizes. The dime is the smallest coin, but it is worth more than a penny or a nickel.

head: Coin
Value
Same as
blocks.cap: What each coin is worth.

blocks.html: A coin’s value comes from its name, not its size. That is why you have to learn each one. A dollar is 100¢: that is 4 quarters, 10 dimes or 20 nickels.

blocks.title: Nickel or dime?
blocks.q: Which is worth more, a nickel or a dime?
steps: A nickel is 5¢. A dime is 10¢.
10 is more than 5, so the dime is worth more, even though it is smaller.

blocks.title: Make 25¢ without a quarter
blocks.q: How can you make 25¢ with dimes and a nickel?

blocks.name: coins
blocks.cap: Your turn: make 25¢ without a quarter.

blocks.html: Penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢. Size does not tell value.
Thinking a nickel is worth more than a dime because it is bigger. Check by saying the values: nickel 5, dime 10.
Grown-up tip: Empty a coin jar and sort the coins together, saying each coin’s name and value.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.C.8 (solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies, using dollar and cent symbols)

blocks.html: To count a pile of coins, line them up from the biggest value to the smallest, then count on. You know the Coin Values.

blocks.name: coins
blocks.cap: Press “Line them up” to sort the coins from greatest to least value, then count on.

blocks.html: Counting the biggest coins first means you start with big jumps and finish with small ones. Change your jump each time the coin changes: 25s for quarters, 10s for dimes, 5s for nickels and 1s for pennies.

blocks.title: Dollars and cents
blocks.q: One one-dollar bill, 1 quarter and 2 dimes
steps: One dollar and 45 cents is written \$1.45.

blocks.html: Sort from greatest to least value, then count on, changing your jump when the coin changes. Write cents with ¢ and dollars with \$.

Counting every coin as 1, or forgetting to switch jumps. With 3 dimes and 2 nickels, “10, 20, 30, 40, 50” keeps counting by 10s for the nickels. Nickels are 5 each: 30, 35, 40. Check: say each coin’s name as you count it.
Grown-up tip: Let your child pay for something small with coins and count out the money.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.C.8 (solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies)

blocks.html: Money stories use adding and subtracting with ¢ and \$. You know how to count money and how to solve word problems.

blocks.name: coins
blocks.cap: A snack costs 63¢ and you pay with \$1. Add coins to count up to \$1.00.

blocks.html: Change is the money you get back. When you pay \$1 (100¢) for something that costs 63¢, the 100¢ is the whole and 63¢ is one part. The change is the other part: $100 - 63$.

blocks.title: Cost together
blocks.q: A pencil costs 35¢ and an eraser costs 48¢. How much for both?

blocks.title: Change from a dollar
blocks.q: A snack costs 63¢. You pay with \$1. How much change do you get?
steps: Count up from 63: +7 to 70, then +30 to 100.

blocks.title: Dollars
blocks.q: Sam has \$20. He buys a book for \$13. How much money is left?

blocks.html: Use the same unit, all cents or all dollars, then add or subtract as the story says. \$1 is 100¢.
Mixing dollars and cents, like thinking \$1 and 25¢ is 26¢. A dollar is 100¢, so \$1 and 25¢ is 125¢, written \$1.25. Check: is the total more than a dollar?
Grown-up tip: At the store, ask your child to figure out the change before the cashier does.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.C.8 (solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies, using dollar and cent symbols)

blocks.html: Graphs show data, the information you collect, as a picture. In Grade 1 you sorted data into groups (Data in Three Groups). Picture graphs and bar graphs make groups easy to compare.

blocks.name: g2-graph
blocks.cap: A picture graph: count the pictures in each row.

blocks.name: g2-graph
blocks.cap: A bar graph. Every line stands for 1, but only every other line has a number.

blocks.html: In a picture graph, each picture is one thing, so you count pictures. In a bar graph, the height of a bar is the number: read straight across from the top of the bar to the numbers on the side. Every grid line counts, even the ones without a number.

blocks.title: Read a bar
steps: The Fish bar stops one line above 6.
Each line is 1 more, so it is 7.

blocks.title: Compare
blocks.q: How many more children have dogs than cats?

blocks.name: g2-graph

task.text: A class voted: Red 4, Blue 6, Green 2. Make the bars match.

blocks.cap: Your turn: build the bar graph with the − and + buttons.

blocks.html: Picture graph: count the pictures. Bar graph: read across from the top of the bar. Then add or subtract to answer questions.
Reading a bar that ends between two numbered lines as the lower number. The Fish bar ends one line above 6, so it shows 7, not 6. Check: count the lines up from the last number you can see.
Grown-up tip: Make a tally of something at home, like the colors of cars passing by, and draw a bar graph together.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.D.10 (draw a picture graph and a bar graph with a single-unit scale to show data with up to four categories)

blocks.html: When you measure many things, a line plot shows all the measurements at once. You need to know how to measure with a ruler and how to read graphs.

blocks.name: g2-graph
blocks.cap: Each X is one pencil. Three pencils are 7 inches long.

blocks.html: A line plot uses a number line marked like a ruler, in the same unit as the measurements. Each measurement gets one X above its number. So you can see at a glance which lengths are common and how far apart the shortest and longest are.

blocks.title: Make the plot
steps: Draw a number line from 3 to 9, with a mark for every inch.
Put one X above each length: one at 4, two at 5, one at 6, three at 7 and one at 8.
Count the Xs: there are 8, one for each pencil.

blocks.title: Read the plot
blocks.q: How much longer is the longest pencil than the shortest?

blocks.html: A line plot puts one X above a number line for each measurement. Count the Xs to answer questions.

Leaving out numbers that have no Xs, so the marks are not evenly spaced. The number line in a line plot must show every number in order, like a ruler. Check: are all the marks the same distance apart?
Grown-up tip: Measure everyone’s hand span or shoe in the family and make a line plot.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.MD.D.9 (generate measurement data to the nearest whole unit and show it in a line plot)

blocks.html: You learned what makes a shape a shape (What Makes a Shape a Shape): sides and corners matter, but color, size and turning don’t. Now you can name shapes by counting.

blocks.name: shapes
blocks.cap: Press “Next shape”. Drag a corner to change the shape and watch its name.

head: Name
Sides
Corners (angles)
blocks.cap: Flat shapes with straight sides.

blocks.html: A corner is where two sides meet, so a closed flat shape always has as many corners as sides. The names count, too: tri- means 3, quad- means 4, penta- means 5 and hexa- means 6.

blocks.name: g2-shapes
blocks.cap: All three are hexagons. Count 6 sides on each one.

blocks.title: Name it
blocks.q: A flat shape has 5 straight sides. What is it?
steps: A shape with 5 sides and 5 corners is a pentagon.

blocks.title: A cube
blocks.q: How many faces does a cube have?
steps: Top, bottom, front, back, left, right: 6 faces.
A cube also has 8 corners (vertices) and 12 edges.

blocks.name: shapes
blocks.cap: Drag to turn the cube, and count its faces, edges and corners.

blocks.html: Name flat shapes by counting sides or corners: 3 triangle, 4 quadrilateral, 5 pentagon, 6 hexagon. A cube has 6 square faces.
Thinking a shape is only a hexagon if it looks like a honeycomb cell. Any closed flat shape with 6 straight sides is a hexagon, even an L-shape like B. Check: count the sides with your finger.
Grown-up tip: Go on a shape hunt: find triangles, quadrilaterals and hexagons around the house, and count their sides.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.G.A.1 (recognize and draw shapes with given attributes; identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons and cubes)

blocks.html: You can cut a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares, like a sheet of stamps or a pan of corn bread. You know about rectangles from Shapes by Sides, Angles and Faces.

blocks.name: arraygrid
blocks.cap: 3 rows and 4 columns of squares. Drag the corner to make other rectangles.

blocks.html: Rows go across and columns go up and down. The squares are all the same size and line up, so every row has the same number of squares. That means you can add the rows instead of counting one by one: $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$.

blocks.title: 2 rows of 5
blocks.q: A rectangle has 2 rows with 5 squares in each row. How many squares?

blocks.title: 3 rows and 3 columns
blocks.q: A rectangle has 3 rows and 3 columns of squares. How many squares?
steps: 3 columns means each row has 3 squares.

blocks.html: A rectangle cut into same-size squares has equal rows. Add the rows (or the columns) to find how many squares there are.
Drawing squares that are not all the same size. For rows and columns to work, every square must match. Check: do the lines go straight across and straight down, evenly spaced?
Grown-up tip: Draw a rectangle on graph paper and cut it into squares together, then count them by rows.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.G.A.2 (partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them)

blocks.html: An array is a set of objects in equal rows. Arrays are the first step toward multiplication, which you will learn in Grade 3 (Arrays). They grow out of Rows and Columns of Squares.

blocks.name: arraygrid
blocks.cap: 4 equal rows of 3: $3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12$. Drag the corner to change the array.

blocks.html: Every row has the same number of objects, so you can add that number again and again, once for each row. Skip counting is a fast way to add equal numbers: 3, 6, 9, 12.

blocks.title: 3 rows of 5
blocks.q: An array has 3 rows with 5 stars in each row. How many stars?

blocks.title: Rows or columns
blocks.q: Show two ways to add an array with 2 rows of 4.
steps: Add the columns: there are 4 columns of 2, so $2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8$.
The total is the same either way.

blocks.html: An array has equal rows. Add the equal rows (or columns), or skip count, to find the total.
Counting every object one by one. It works, but it is slow and easy to lose your place. Add the rows instead: 4 rows of 3 is $3 + 3 + 3 + 3$. Check by adding the columns, too.
Grown-up tip: Look for arrays in egg cartons, muffin pans and windows, and add them by rows.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.OA.C.4 (use addition to find the total in a rectangular array with up to 5 rows and 5 columns)

blocks.html: In Grade 1 you cut shapes into Halves and Fourths. Now you will cut them into thirds, too.

blocks.name: g2-shapes
blocks.cap: The same circle cut into 2, 3 and 4 equal shares, with one share shaded. More shares means smaller shares.

blocks.html: Equal shares are the same size, so everyone gets a fair amount. A whole is 2 halves, 3 thirds or 4 fourths. When you share with more people, each person gets less, so a fourth is smaller than a third, and a third is smaller than a half.

blocks.name: g2-shapes
blocks.cap: A and B are both cut into halves. C is not: one part is bigger.

blocks.title: Halves that look different
blocks.q: Square B is cut from corner to corner. Are the two parts halves?
steps: The two triangles are the same size: one would fit exactly on top of the other.
So yes, they are halves, even though they are a different shape from the halves of A.

blocks.title: Which share is bigger?
blocks.q: Which is bigger: a half or a fourth of the same pizza?
steps: A half is 1 of 2 equal shares. A fourth is 1 of 4 equal shares.

blocks.html: Equal shares are the same size. Two equal shares are halves, three are thirds and four are fourths (or quarters). A whole is 2 halves, 3 thirds or 4 fourths.

Thinking equal shares must be the same shape. The halves of square B are triangles and the halves of A are rectangles, but each one is exactly half of the same square. Check: same size, not same shape.
Grown-up tip: Cut sandwiches or toast into halves, thirds or fourths in different ways, and ask whether the shares are fair.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2, standard 2.G.A.3 (partition circles and rectangles into two, three or four equal shares; equal shares need not have the same shape)
